I've farmed this land for over thirty years, and the decision is the same as it's always been: winter wheat and summer maize in rotation. That's what this land wants, that's what the market absorbs, and that's what I know how to grow well. My fields are on the North China Plain — deep loam, groundwater accessible — so I'm not fighting the land, I'm working with it.

I have about 20 mu total. All of it goes into the wheat-maize rotation. I tried cotton for a few years in my thirties, and the price volatility nearly broke me. I'm not doing that again at 55.

For the winter wheat (planted this coming October, harvested June), I'll use Jimai 22 — it's an improved variety with good disease resistance and the yield trials in Handan have been solid. I went to the county extension office last month and the soil test showed my phosphorus is adequate, so I'll pull back slightly from what I did last year. I'll irrigate four times: at sowing to ensure germination, over-winter watering to protect the root system, jointing stage which is the most critical, and at heading to protect grain fill. Three pesticide passes — herbicide in the fall, a spring herbicide with growth regulator, and a fungicide at heading for powdery mildew.

For summer maize after the wheat harvest in June, I go straight to no-tillage direct seeding — it saves time during the narrow planting window and holds soil moisture. I use Zhengdan 958, the hybrid that's been reliable here for fifteen years. The July monsoon rains carry most of the irrigation load; I'll only supplement twice. Two pesticide applications — one herbicide after emergence and one for corn borer and aphids around silking.
